dv.{{raw:headline}}: Neither improver beat two plain attempts on ARC-AGI-2

blocks.orig_inner: Can an AI coach teach itself to coach better?
blocks.md: Can an AI coach teach itself to coach better?

blocks.orig_inner: Picture two AIs. The player solves visual logic puzzles. The coach studies where the player goes wrong and rewrites the player's code to make it better. The twist: we also let the coach rewrite its own code, so it could learn to coach better. Then we tested whether a self-improved coach actually trains better players.
blocks.md: Picture two AIs. The **player** solves visual logic puzzles. The **coach** studies where the player goes wrong and rewrites the player's code to make it better. The twist: we also let the coach rewrite *its own* code, so it could learn to coach better. Then we tested whether a self-improved coach actually trains better players.

blocks.orig_inner: Short answer: no. On a final exam of 120 puzzles none of them had seen before, coached players scored about the same as a player with no coaching at all. What did help was much simpler: letting the model think longer before answering beat every kind of coaching.
blocks.md: Short answer: no. On a final exam of {{int:sets.heldout_tasks}} puzzles none of them had seen before, coached players scored about the same as a player with no coaching at all. What did help was much simpler: letting the model think longer before answering beat every kind of coaching.

blocks.orig_inner: How the experiment works
blocks.md: How the experiment works

blocks.orig_inner: The player is a short program that solves each puzzle using at most two calls to an AI model.11In the repository, the "player" is the task agent and the "coach" is the meta agent. Both run on the same model. The coach runs on the same model. It looks at how the player did on 25 practice puzzles, then edits the player's code to fix what went wrong. One round of this (play, review, edit) is called a generation. In step 1, the coach is also allowed to edit its own code, so in principle it can get better at coaching.
blocks.md: The player is a short program that solves each puzzle using at most two calls to an AI model.[^1] The coach runs on the same model. It looks at how the player did on {{int:sets.source_practice_tasks}} practice puzzles, then edits the player's code to fix what went wrong. One round of this (play, review, edit) is called a **generation**. In step 1, the coach is also allowed to edit its own code, so in principle it can get better at coaching.

blocks.orig_inner: A coach edits the player's code. Then we let the coach edit its own.
blocks.md: A coach edits the player's code. Then we let the coach edit its own.

blocks.orig_inner: Step 1: the coach improves itself over many generations. Step 2: we freeze it and see how well it trains a brand-new player.
blocks.md: Step 1: the coach improves itself over many generations. Step 2: we freeze it and see how well it trains a brand-new player.

blocks.orig_inner: Figure 1: how the experiment works.
blocks.md: **Figure 1**: how the experiment works.

blocks.orig_inner: We ran step 1 6 separate times, for 12 generations each. To test a coach, we froze it so it could no longer change (either the original coach or the self-improved coach picked at generation 12 of each run, the generation-12 coach22From each run we took the self-edited coach whose players improved most on practice. This rule was fixed before any exam result existed.). We then handed it a fresh, untouched player and gave it 8 rounds of coaching on a different set of 25 practice puzzles. The finished player sat the exam exactly once: 120 puzzles it had never seen.33The 120 public ARC-AGI-2 evaluation tasks [1], with 167 test inputs. A puzzle with several test inputs earns partial credit.
blocks.md: We ran step 1 {{int:n_source_seeds}} separate times, for {{int:derived.sourceGens}} generations each. To test a coach, we froze it so it could no longer change (either the original coach or the self-improved coach picked at generation 12 of each run, the **generation-12 coach**[^2]). We then handed it a fresh, untouched player and gave it {{int:derived.rounds}} rounds of coaching on a different set of {{int:sets.payoff_practice_tasks}} practice puzzles. The finished player sat the exam exactly once: {{int:sets.heldout_tasks}} puzzles it had never seen.[^3]

blocks.orig_inner: We also needed something to compare against. The uncoached player sat the same exam as it was, and once more with the model set to think longer: one notch higher on its "reasoning effort" setting, which lets the model reason more before it answers. It still got only two calls and two answers per puzzle. That setting was locked, so no coach could change it.44A gateway that no agent could edit fixed the model, its reasoning effort (high; xhigh for the think-longer run), the call cap and the budget.
blocks.md: We also needed something to compare against. The uncoached player sat the same exam as it was, and once more with the model set to **think longer**: one notch higher on its "reasoning effort" setting, which lets the model reason more before it answers. It still got only two calls and two answers per puzzle. That setting was locked, so no coach could change it.[^4]

blocks.orig_inner: Players trained by the original coach scored +0.4 points above the uncoached player, and players trained by a generation-12 coach −1.4 points. Both gaps are smaller than ordinary run-to-run noise, the amount scores bounce around when you simply run the same setup again. In other words, we can't tell either one apart from no effect.5595% intervals: original coach minus no coach [−1.9, +2.8] points; generation-12 coach minus no coach [−4.0, +1.3]; generation-12 coach minus original −1.8 [−4.2, +0.6]. All include zero, which means "no difference" fits the data. Welch t-intervals [2]; the headline was pre-registered. Thinking longer, by contrast, added about 12 points.

blocks.orig_inner: How well does a coach improve, and does it get better at improving?
blocks.md: How well does a coach improve, and does it get better at improving?

blocks.orig_inner: Agent plasticity is how efficiently an agent turns experience into gains on tasks it has not seen [3]. Here we measure it one level up, for the coach.
blocks.md: **Agent plasticity** is how efficiently an agent turns experience into gains on tasks it has not seen [[3]](#ref-plasticity "cite"). Here we measure it one level up, for the coach.

blocks.orig_inner: First-order plasticity: how well a coach improves the player. Freeze a coach, let it improve a fresh player for 8 rounds, and compare that player's exam score with the uncoached player's. This is the improvement@k measure from the Hyperagents paper [4], with k = 8 rounds. The original coach: +0.4 points (95% interval [−1.9, +2.8]).
blocks.md: **First-order plasticity: how well a coach improves the player.** Freeze a coach, let it improve a fresh player for {{int:derived.rounds}} rounds, and compare that player's exam score with the uncoached player's. This is the *improvement@k* measure from the Hyperagents paper [[4]](#ref-hyper "cite"), with k = {{int:derived.rounds}} rounds. The original coach: {{pts:G.est}} points (95% interval {{ci:G}}).

blocks.orig_inner: Second-order plasticity: whether the coach gets better at improving. Does that first-order gain grow as the coach rewrites itself? Compare players trained by later coaches with players trained by the original coach. Generation-12 coach minus original: −1.8 points (95% interval [−4.2, +0.6]). Generation-40 coaches minus original: +0.6 points (95% interval [−6.5, +7.8]).
blocks.md: **Second-order plasticity: whether the coach gets better at improving.** Does that first-order gain grow as the coach rewrites itself? Compare players trained by later coaches with players trained by the original coach. Generation-12 coach minus original: {{pts:Delta.est}} points (95% interval {{ci:Delta}}). Generation-40 coaches minus original: {{pts:extension.gen40_minus_gen0.est}} points (95% interval {{ci:extension.gen40_minus_gen0}}).

blocks.orig_inner: Here both are indistinguishable from zero: coaching did not measurably improve the player, and rewriting itself did not make the coach a better coach. “Second-order plasticity” is our own name; the Hyperagents paper calls a coach rewriting itself metacognitive self-modification. That paper's positive result comes from moving evolved coaches to a new kind of task. Ours is a same-task test on ARC-AGI-2, so it does not directly test that claim.

blocks.orig_inner: Did more generations help?
blocks.md: Did more generations help?

blocks.orig_inner: One reason it didn't: coaches rarely changed themselves. A coach's own code changed in only 21 of 72 generations. We then ran a follow-up that wasn't in the original pre-registered plan (its own plan was written down before it ran). In it, 4 runs kept going to generation 40, and we also tested coaches picked at generations 20 and 40. Like the generation-12 coach in the main result, these are self-improved coaches, picked by almost the same rule, just from a later point in each run (the follow-up rule also asked for at least 3 versions built on the coach). Often the later pick was literally the same code: in run 1, the coaches picked at generations 12, 20 and 40 were all one version, made back at generation 1.

blocks.orig_inner: The main study didn't record what the model was thinking. So afterwards we re-ran one coaching round with the model's reasoning summaries saved, so you can follow the player and the coach step by step. This is a separate demo to show how coaching works; it isn't part of the results. One caveat: these aren't the model's raw thoughts. The API returns only a summary of its hidden reasoning (which can run to thousands of words), the summary can be lossy or garbled, and only some calls returned one.66Same model, reasoning effort, call cap and practice puzzles as the study, with one difference: the demo asked for “detailed” reasoning summaries, while the study asked for “auto” (which returned none in a short test). We show the only round, out of several tried, that changed the player without breaking it, plus two puzzles picked to illustrate: one the edit fixed and one it didn't. Runs aren't deterministic, so each player was run on each puzzle several times.

blocks.orig_inner: The original coach needed adapting. With the repository's instruction as written, the model only asked clarifying questions. We added one sentence ("work autonomously") and made tool-call parsing more forgiving. Both kinds of coach started from this adapted version.
blocks.md: **The original coach needed adapting.** With the repository's instruction as written, the model only asked clarifying questions. We added one sentence ("work autonomously") and made tool-call parsing more forgiving. Both kinds of coach started from this adapted version.

blocks.orig_inner: The original coach often made no edit. It ended 11 of its first 31 rounds without one, mostly because of tool-call formatting problems. As pre-registered, we left this as it was.
blocks.md: **The original coach often made no edit.** It ended 11 of its first 31 rounds without one, mostly because of tool-call formatting problems. As pre-registered, we left this as it was.

blocks.orig_inner: Some coach edits broke the player. One edit passed an argument the function didn't accept, and that player scored 0. Results like this still count.
blocks.md: **Some coach edits broke the player.** One edit passed an argument the function didn't accept, and that player scored 0. Results like this still count.

blocks.orig_inner: Re-runs. Bugs in the test harness forced restarts of two original-coach test runs (one of them twice) and cost one self-improvement run a generation. An early 30-minute time limit cut off 49 exam answers for the no-coach and think-longer players; all were re-run with a 2 to 3 hour limit (think longer: 39.9% before, 41.1% after). Six machine restarts lost no results.
